title: Collecting on a court order
intro: Winning a court order does not always mean the money is paid. This guide describes the enforcement steps the court rules and statutes set out in Small Claims Court, the Superior Court of Justice (civil), and for family support orders.

sections.heading: A judgment is not automatic payment
paragraphs: The ontario.ca guide explains: “A judgment is an order of the court; it is not a guarantee of payment.” CLEO adds that “the court does not collect the money for you.” Taking steps to collect is called enforcing the judgment. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment; CLEO, Steps to Justice: How do I collect the money I'm owed?)

The court rules use two terms. A “creditor” is “a person who is entitled to enforce an order for the payment or recovery of money”. A “debtor” is “a person against whom an order for the payment or recovery of money may be enforced.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.01; Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.01)

Under the Limitations Act, 2002, “There is no limitation period in respect of” “a proceeding to enforce an order of a court, or any other order that may be enforced in the same way as an order of a court” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 16 (1) (b); Rules of the Small Claims Court, rr. 20.06 (1.1), 20.07 (1.1), 20.08 (2.1); Rules of Civil Procedure, rr. 60.07 (2), 60.08 (2))

The court rules still require the court's permission (leave) for some enforcement steps once six years have passed since the order, as described below. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 16 (1) (b); Rules of the Small Claims Court, rr. 20.06 (1.1), 20.07 (1.1), 20.08 (2.1); Rules of Civil Procedure, rr. 60.07 (2), 60.08 (2))

sections.heading: Small Claims Court: the tools and first steps
paragraphs: “In addition to any other method of enforcement provided by law”, a Small Claims order for the payment or recovery of money may be enforced by a writ of seizure and sale of personal property (Form 20C), a writ of seizure and sale of land (Form 20D), and garnishment. A further order as to payment may also be made after an examination. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.03)

The guide says: “You can start taking enforcement steps immediately after judgment is given.” It says “the best place to start is often with a simple written request for payment”, and notes that a creditor who does not know where the debtor banks, works or what the debtor owns “could begin the enforcement process by requesting an examination hearing.” (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

If the debtor lives or carries on business in the area of a different court, the guide says a Certificate of Judgment (Form 20A) is needed before that court can issue a notice of garnishment or notice of examination. If there is default under the order, the clerk issues it on the creditor's request, supported by an affidavit for enforcement request (Form 20P) “stating the amount still owing”. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.04 (1); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

After judgment, the guide explains that “post-judgment interest accrues automatically” on the amount owing under the judgment. It describes this as “simple (not compound) interest”, recalculated as payments reduce the balance. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

The guide also notes that “The orders of some boards, tribunals and agencies, as well as other levels of court in Ontario can be filed and enforced in the Small Claims Court”, for example orders under the Residential Tenancies Act and the Employment Standards Act. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

sections.heading: Small Claims Court: the examination hearing
paragraphs: If there is default under a payment order, the clerk of a court in the territorial division where the debtor or other person to be examined “resides or carries on business” shall, at the creditor's request, issue a notice of examination (Form 20H). The request is supported by an affidavit for enforcement request (Form 20P), and a certificate of judgment if the order was made elsewhere. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.10 (1), (2))

The debtor and other persons may be examined about “the reason for nonpayment”, “the debtor's income and property”, “the debts owed to and by the debtor”, any disposal of property before or after the order, “the debtor's present, past and future means to satisfy the order”, whether the debtor intends to obey the order, and “any other matter pertinent to the enforcement of the order.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.10 (4))

A debtor who is an individual must complete a financial information form (Form 20I), serve it on the creditor but “not file it with the court”, and provide a copy to the judge. The debtor brings documents that support it. An officer or director of a corporate debtor may be examined on its behalf. The examination is held in the absence of the public unless the court orders otherwise, “conducted under oath” and “recorded.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.10 (4.1), (4.2), (5), (6))

According to the guide, the creditor serves the notice of examination “at least 30 days before the hearing”, together with a blank Financial Information Form if the debtor is an individual, and files an affidavit of service “at least 3 days prior to the date set for the examination.” (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

“After the examination or if the debtor's consent is filed, the court may make an order as to payment.” While that order is in force, a creditor named in it may take no other enforcement step “except issuing a writ of seizure and sale of land and filing it with the sheriff.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.10 (7), (8))

If a person served with a notice of examination does not attend, or attends but refuses to answer questions or produce documents, the court may order a contempt hearing. At that hearing the court may order the person to attend an examination, or “be jailed for a period of not more than five days”, among other orders. The guide notes: “Paying the debt does not expunge (remove) the contempt.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.11 (1), (2), (7); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

sections.heading: Small Claims Court: garnishment
paragraphs: “A creditor may enforce an order for the payment or recovery of money by garnishment of debts payable to the debtor by other persons.” The guide says: “Most often, people garnish wages or bank accounts.” The person who owes money to the debtor, such as a bank or employer, is the garnishee. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (1); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

The creditor files an affidavit for enforcement request (Form 20P) “naming one debtor and one garnishee” with the clerk of a court in the territorial division where the debtor resides or carries on business. The clerk then issues a notice of garnishment (Form 20E). A separate notice is needed for each garnishee. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (3), (4), (5); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

The creditor serves the notice on the garnishee, and on the debtor “within five days of serving it on the garnishee.” If the garnishee is a financial institution, notices are served “at the branch at which the debt is payable.” The guide says a blank Garnishee's Statement (Form 20F) is served on the garnishee. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (6.1), (6.2); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

The garnishee must pay the clerk what it owes the debtor, up to the amount in the notice, within 10 days after service or 10 days after the debt becomes payable, “whichever is later.” This includes debts payable within six years after the notice is issued. Payments cannot exceed the portion of wages subject to garnishment under section 7 of the Wages Act. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (7), (8), (9))

CLEO states: “You cannot garnish more than 20 percent of a person's wages.” That CLEO page was last reviewed on February 23, 2017. The guide says “employment insurance, social assistance and pension payments cannot be garnished, even if the funds have been deposited into an account at a financial institution.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: Can the court take money from someone's bank account if I have a court order against them?; ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

If a debt is payable to the debtor and co-owners, such as a joint account, “one-half of the indebtedness” or another amount set by the court may be garnished. A co-owner served with a notice to co-owner of debt may dispute only by requesting a garnishment hearing “within 30 days after the notice is sent.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (2), (16))

A creditor, debtor, garnishee, co-owner or other interested person may ask the clerk to schedule a garnishment hearing. The court may decide rights and liabilities, and “vary or suspend periodic payments under a notice of garnishment”. The guide says a debtor facing “real financial hardship” may ask a judge to increase the exempt portion of wages. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (15), (15.2); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

Once proof of service on the debtor is filed, and unless a hearing or certain motions or requests are pending, the clerk pays out the first payment 30 days after receiving it and later payments as received, shared equally among creditors who filed garnishments and are not yet paid in full. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (10), (20), (20.1))

A notice of garnishment lasts “six years from the date of its issue” and may be renewed. Leave is needed to issue one if more than six years have passed since the order or enforcement is conditional. When the debt is paid, the creditor serves a notice of termination (Form 20R). (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (2.1), (5.1), (20.2))

sections.heading: Small Claims Court: seizing property and writs of delivery
paragraphs: On default, the clerk issues to a bailiff, at the creditor's request with an affidavit for enforcement request, a writ of seizure and sale of personal property (Form 20C). The bailiff enforces it “for the amount owing, postjudgment interest and the bailiff's fees and expenses.” The creditor may file a direction to enforce (Form 20O). Seized goods are not sold unless notice is mailed “at least 10 days before the sale” and advertised. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.06 (1), (4), (6))

The guide notes that under the Execution Act a debtor has certain exemptions from seizure, such as clothing and household furniture “up to a certain amount”, and that “The debtor has a right to choose the goods that make up the exemptions.” The creditor pays an enforcement fee and a deposit, and the enforcement office “can refuse to act if the estimated costs of executing the writ of seizure and sale are greater than the debtor's equity”. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

For land, the clerk issues a writ of seizure and sale of land (Form 20D) to the sheriff the creditor names. Once issued, the Rules of Civil Procedure apply to it as if it were issued under rule 60.07. The guide says a writ filed in a county or district encumbers land the debtor owns there now or buys later, and a separate writ is needed for each location. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.07 (1), (2); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

The guide explains that four months after the writ is filed the creditor can direct the sheriff to seize and sell the land, “but the actual sale cannot proceed until the writ has been on file for six months.” The Rules of Civil Procedure contain the same four-month and six-month limits. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment; Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.07 (17), (18))

Both writs expire “on the sixth anniversary of the date of its issue” unless renewed; a request to renew (Form 20N) is filed with the bailiff or sheriff before the writ expires (a land writ may instead be renewed under the Rules of Civil Procedure). If more than six years have passed since the order, either writ “may be issued only with leave of the court.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.06 (1.1), (2), (3), 20.07 (1.1), (3), (4))

“An order for the delivery of personal property may be enforced by a writ of delivery (Form 20B)” issued by the clerk to a bailiff, supported by an affidavit that the property has not been delivered. If the property cannot be found or taken, the person may bring a motion for an order directing the bailiff to seize other personal property of the person against whom the order was made. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.05 (1), (2))

sections.heading: Small Claims Court: limits on enforcement and full payment
paragraphs: The court may stay enforcement “for such time and on such terms as are just”, and may vary the times and amounts of payment “if it is satisfied that the debtor's circumstances have changed.” While an order for periodic payment is in force, a named creditor may take no other step except issuing and filing a writ of seizure and sale of land. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.02 (1), (2))

If the debtor misses payments under a periodic payment order, the creditor may serve a notice of default of payment (Form 20L) and file it with an affidavit of default of payment (Form 20M). The order “terminates on the day that is 15 days after” service, unless a consent (Form 13B) waiving the default is filed within that period. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.02 (3), (4))

“A debtor against whom there are two or more unsatisfied orders for the payment of money may make a motion to the court for a consolidation order.” The motion is served on each creditor “at least seven days before the hearing date.” The order ends immediately after 21 days of default, and then no new consolidation order may be made for one year. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.09 (1), (3), (10), (11))

When the order is paid in full, a party may file a request for clerk's order on consent (Form 11.2A) if all parties consent, or the debtor may bring a motion for an order confirming full payment. The guide says that a creditor who has used any of the enforcement processes is responsible for telling the court and the enforcement office(s) when the debt has been paid in full. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.12; ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

sections.heading: Superior Court of Justice (civil): Rule 60
paragraphs: “In addition to any other method of enforcement provided by law”, a civil order for the payment or recovery of money may be enforced by a writ of seizure and sale (Form 60A), garnishment, a writ of sequestration (Form 60B), and “the appointment of a receiver.” An order to do or not do an act, other than pay money, may be enforced by a contempt order. (Rules of Civil Procedure, rr. 60.02 (1), 60.05)

A creditor obtains a writ of seizure and sale by filing a requisition with the registrar, with the order “as entered”. Leave is needed if “six years or more have elapsed since the date of the order”. A writ “expires on the sixth anniversary of the date of its issue” unless renewed; a writ filed with a sheriff is renewed by filing a request to renew (Form 60E). (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.07 (1), (2), (6), (8))

For garnishment, the creditor files a requisition for garnishment (Form 60G) and an affidavit, and the registrar issues a notice of garnishment (Form 60H) naming “one debtor and one garnishee.” The garnishee pays the sheriff, “less $10 for the cost of making each payment”, within the ten-day periods in the rule, subject to section 7 of the Wages Act. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.08 (4), (6), (6.1), (11), (14))

For a bank, a garnished debt does not include “money in an account opened after the notice of garnishment is served”. A garnishee who disputes must serve and file a garnishee's statement (Form 60I) within 10 days. Any interested person may move for a garnishment hearing, and the sheriff suspends payments to the creditor until the motion is decided. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.08 (13), (15), (16), (16.1.1))

Under rule 60.18, a creditor may examine the debtor about the same matters listed in the Small Claims rule, including “the debtor's income and property”. “Only one examination under subrule (2) or (3) may be held in a twelve month period in respect of a debtor in the same proceeding, unless the court orders otherwise.” The court may also order others with knowledge to be examined. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.18 (2), (4), (6))

If an examination shows that a debtor “has concealed or made away with property to defeat or defraud creditors, a judge may make a contempt order against the debtor.” The notice of examination is served on the debtor personally or by an alternative to personal service. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.18 (5), (7))

A writ of sequestration “may be issued only with leave of the court”, and only where the court “is satisfied that other enforcement measures are or are likely to be ineffective.” A party entitled to enforce an order is entitled to the costs of enforcement steps “on a partial indemnity scale, unless the court on motion orders otherwise”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, rr. 60.09 (1), (2), 60.19 (1))

sections.heading: Family support orders: the Family Responsibility Office
paragraphs: The Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996 creates the “Director of the Family Responsibility Office”. “It is the duty of the Director to enforce support orders where the support order and the related support deduction order, if any, are filed in the Director’s office and to pay the amounts collected to the person to whom they are owed.” (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, ss. 2, 5 (1))

“An Ontario court that makes a support order, as defined in subsection 1 (1), shall also make a support deduction order.” It must be made “even though the court cannot identify an income source”, but not for a provisional order. The clerk or registrar files both orders with the Director’s office “promptly after it is signed.” (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, ss. 10 (1), (4), (5), 12 (1), (2))

The Director may serve notice of a support deduction order on each income source, such as an employer. The income source deducts the support owed and pays it to the Director, starting no later than the first payment to the payor that falls “at least 14 days after” service (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, ss. 20 (2), 22 (1), (2), 23 (1), (3))

Deductions “shall not exceed 50 per cent of the net amount owed by the income source to the payor”, but up to 100 per cent of an income tax refund or other lump sum attachable under federal law may be deducted. (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, ss. 20 (2), 22 (1), (2), 23 (1), (3))

Until deductions begin, or if they stop, the payor must pay the Director if the order is filed there, or the recipient if it is not. A support order and support deduction order “may be withdrawn at any time” by written notice, unless the order says they cannot be. Withdrawal needs the recipient's signature, and the payor's too if the payor is in compliance. (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, ss. 16 (1), (1.1), 22 (3))

When a filed support order is in default, the Director may serve a first notice that the payor’s driver’s licence may be suspended unless, within 30 days, the payor makes a satisfactory arrangement, obtains and files an order to refrain, or pays all arrears. The Director may also require the payor to appear at a default hearing, where the payor is presumed able to pay “unless the contrary is shown”. (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, ss. 34, 41 (1), (9))

Part VI of the Act lists other enforcement mechanisms, including registration of a support order against land, writs of seizure and sale, garnishment of joint accounts and lottery prizes, and reporting default to a consumer reporting agency. (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, ss. 42 to 47)

sections.heading: Family Law Rules: enforcing a family order
paragraphs: Under rule 26, a payment order may be enforced by a request for a financial statement, a request for disclosure from an income source, a financial examination, seizure and sale, garnishment, “a default hearing (rule 30), if the order is a support order”, the appointment of a receiver, and registration under section 42 of the Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996. (Family Law Rules, r. 26 (2), (3))

An order other than a payment order may be enforced by “a writ of temporary seizure of property”, “a contempt order (rule 31)”, and the appointment of a receiver. A statement of money owed is in Form 26, with a copy of the order in default attached. (Family Law Rules, r. 26 (4), (5))

If the Director enforces an order, the rules about enforcement by the person the order favours apply to the Director. A recipient who files a support order with the Director must, on the Director's request, assign any enforcement already started to the Director. If the parties withdraw the order, the Director assigns its enforcement to the recipient if the recipient asks at the same time as giving the notice of withdrawal. (Family Law Rules, r. 26 (10), (12), (13))

If a payment order is in default, the recipient may serve an appointment for a financial examination (Form 27C). The payor must attend, bring the named documents, and serve a financial statement (Form 13) “not later than seven days before the date of the examination.” (Family Law Rules, r. 27 (11))

When a support order not filed with the Director is in default, the recipient may file a request with the court with a statement of arrears. The clerk then requires the payor “to file a financial statement and appear before the court to explain the default.” (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, s. 41 (2))
